title: Drilling fluids in one page
points: Jobs of mud: carry cuttings, control pressure, cool and lubricate the bit, stabilize the hole, transmit hydraulic power and data.
Water-base mud is cheapest; oil- and synthetic-base (invert emulsion) muds win in reactive shale, HPHT and high-angle wells.
Bingham model: PV = θ<sub>600</sub> − θ<sub>300</sub> (cp); YP = θ<sub>300</sub> − PV (lbf/100 ft²).
Barite (SG ≈ 4.2) raises density; bentonite and polymers build viscosity and fluid-loss control.
Solids control order: shaker → (degasser) → desander → desilter → centrifuge.
Losses: seepage (< 10 bbl/hr), partial, total. Treat with LCM, lower ECD, or cement.
tip: 0.052 converts ppg × ft into psi. Learn it by heart; half of well-control math uses it.

title: Geophysics essentials
points: Reflections happen where acoustic impedance (ρ·V) changes.
P-waves travel through solids and fluids; S-waves only through solids.
Processing chain: geometry → deconvolution → velocity analysis → NMO → stack → migration.
Vertical resolution ≈ λ/4, where λ = V/f. Deeper data has lower frequency, so resolution gets worse.
Bright spots and AVO can flag gas, but always check them against well data.
Well ties use a synthetic seismogram built from sonic and density logs, or a VSP.
tip: Two-way time: always divide by 2 before you multiply by velocity.

title: Petroleum geology
points: A petroleum system needs a source, migration, reservoir, seal and trap, in the right order in time.
Traps are structural (anticline, fault), stratigraphic (pinch-out, reef, unconformity) or a mix of both.
Oil window ≈ 60–120 °C; hotter source rock makes gas.
Sandstone porosity is mostly between the grains; carbonates add vugs and fractures, and diagenesis can change them a lot.
Normal hydrostatic gradient ≈ 0.433 psi/ft (fresh water) to 0.465 psi/ft (brine).
Cuttings, cores and mud-log gas shows are the geologist's direct evidence while drilling.
tip: Mnemonic SMRST: Source, Migration, Reservoir, Seal, Trap, then add timing.

title: Formation evaluation quick sheet
points: Gamma ray: shale high, clean sand low. SP shows permeable beds.
Resistivity: hydrocarbons are high, salt water is low. Deep resistivity ≈ R<sub>t</sub>.
Density and neutron give porosity; gas shows as a crossover (density φ > neutron φ).
Archie's equation works for clean (shale-free) rock; shaly sands need corrections such as Simandoux.
Net pay = rock that passes the porosity, V<sub>sh</sub> and S<sub>w</sub> cutoffs.
Formation testers give pressure gradients that reveal fluid types and contacts.
tip: Sandstone matrix density is 2.65 g/cc, limestone 2.71 and dolomite 2.87.

title: Drilling and well control
points: Primary well control is the mud's hydrostatic pressure; secondary well control is the BOP.
Kick signs: pit gain, flow with the pumps off, a drilling break, rising return flow, falling pump pressure.
Shut in, record SIDPP and SICP, then kill with the driller's method or wait and weight.
The mud weight window lies between pore pressure and fracture gradient, checked with a LOT or FIT.
BHA: bit, motor or RSS, MWD/LWD, stabilizers, collars.
Stuck-pipe causes: differential, packoff or bridging, wellbore geometry.
equations: ICP = SCR + SIDPP;   FCP = SCR × KMW / MW
tip: Use TVD for pressure and MD for volume.

title: Completions
points: Completion options: open hole, cased and perforated, slotted liner, screens, multizone or intelligent.
Sand control: screens, gravel pack, frac pack, chemical consolidation.
Safety barriers: SSSV, packer, tubing, tree.
Stimulation: matrix acid (below frac pressure) versus hydraulic fracturing (above).
Completion brines must give overbalance without damaging the rock (NaCl, CaCl<sub>2</sub>, CaBr<sub>2</sub>, formates).
equations: q = kh(p<sub>e</sub> − p<sub>wf</sub>) / [141.2 B μ (ln(r<sub>e</sub>/r<sub>w</sub>) + s)]
tip: Negative skin is good: a fracture or acid job can take skin down to about −3 to −5.

title: Workover and intervention
points: Light intervention: slickline, wireline. Medium: coiled tubing. Heavy: workover rig or snubbing.
Typical reasons: sand fill, scale, water or gas breakthrough, failed equipment, recompletion.
Kill the well before pulling tubing, or work live with snubbing or coiled tubing.
Plug and abandonment: cement plugs set over reservoirs and casing shoes, then tested.
Through-tubing work avoids the cost of pulling the completion.
tip: 1029.4 turns inches² into bbl/ft. Use it for every displacement volume.

title: Enhanced oil recovery
points: Primary (natural drive) → secondary (water or gas injection) → tertiary (EOR).
Thermal methods (steam, combustion) lower viscosity; best for heavy oil.
Gas methods (CO<sub>2</sub>, hydrocarbon, N<sub>2</sub>) swell the oil, lower its viscosity and can become miscible.
Chemical methods: polymer fixes mobility; surfactant or alkali cut IFT to move residual oil.
Overall efficiency = displacement efficiency × areal sweep × vertical sweep.
tip: M < 1 is stable (good); M > 1 means fingering.

title: Production testing
points: A test separator or multiphase meter measures each well's oil, gas and water rates.
A DST is a temporary completion on the drillstring: flow, shut in, sample.
Fluid samples: bottomhole (single phase, best) or recombined separator samples.
Report GOR, water cut, BS&W and API gravity, plus choke and pressures.
Gas deliverability: back-pressure, isochronal or modified isochronal tests give the AOF.
tip: Water has SG 1.0, which is 10 °API.

title: Well testing (pressure transient)
points: On a derivative plot: wellbore storage first (unit slope), then radial flow (flat derivative), then boundaries.
Buildup: shut in a producer. Falloff: shut in an injector. Interference: watch an observation well.
Semilog slope m gives kh; the offset at 1 hour gives skin.
Horner extrapolation to (t<sub>p</sub> + Δt)/Δt = 1 gives p*.
Radius of investigation grows with the square root of time.
equations: s = 1.151 [(p<sub>1hr</sub> − p<sub>wf</sub>)/m − log(k/(φ μ c<sub>t</sub> r<sub>w</sub>²)) + 3.23]
r<sub>i</sub> = √(k t / (948 φ μ c<sub>t</sub>))   (ft, hr)
tip: On a derivative plot a flat line means radial flow. That's where you read k.

title: Reservoir characterization
points: Combine seismic, logs, cores and tests into one static model.
Geostatistics: variograms and kriging or stochastic simulation honor the well data.
Run several realizations to capture uncertainty (P90, P50, P10).
Upscale the fine model to a simulation grid, then history-match it.
Drive mechanisms ranked by typical recovery: water drive > gas cap > solution gas.
equations: N = 7758 A h φ (1 − S<sub>wi</sub>) / B<sub>oi</sub>   (STB; acres, ft)
G = 43,560 A h φ (1 − S<sub>wi</sub>) / B<sub>gi</sub>   (scf; B<sub>gi</sub> in ft³/scf)
tip: 7758 bbl in one acre-ft and 43,560 ft³ in one acre-ft are the two constants that come up again and again.

title: Production logging
points: Standard toolstring: spinner, density, capacitance or holdup, temperature, pressure, gamma ray and CCL.
Make several passes up and down at different speeds to calibrate the spinner.
Holdup differs from the flow fraction because of slip between the phases.
Temperature shows entries: gas cools as it expands, liquid entries warm the well.
Cased-hole saturation: pulsed neutron. Cement quality: CBL or VDL, ultrasonic tools.
tip: Read flow profiles from the bottom up: each step in the spinner is a zone contributing.

title: Production facilities
points: Separation, treating, storage and transfer: separator → FWKO or treater → stock tank → LACT.
Gas processing: dehydration (glycol), sweetening (amine), compression.
Produced water: treat (skimmers, flotation, hydrocyclones) then reinject or dispose.
Flow assurance threats: hydrates, wax, asphaltenes, scale, corrosion.
Safety: relief valves, ESD systems and the flare.
tip: Hydrate avoidance: keep the fluid warm, keep it dry, or add MEG or methanol.

title: Production engineering
points: Nodal analysis: the well's rate is where the IPR (inflow) meets the tubing curve (outflow).
Above the bubblepoint the IPR is a straight line (PI); below it, use Vogel.
Lift choices: gas lift (gassy, deviated wells), ESP (high rate), rod pump (low rate, onshore), PCP (viscous oil, sand).
Decline curves: exponential (b = 0), hyperbolic (0 < b < 1), harmonic (b = 1).
Watch water cut, GOR and pressure. They show coning, breakthrough and depletion.
tip: Vogel needs only one test point plus the reservoir pressure to draw the whole curve.

title: Shale gas and unconventionals
points: Key rock properties: TOC, maturity (R<sub>o</sub>), brittleness, thickness, pressure.
Horizontal laterals plus multistage fracturing (plug and perf or sleeves).
Gas storage: free gas in pores plus adsorbed gas (Langmuir).
Steep first-year decline, so EUR comes from type curves (often hyperbolic with b > 1 early on).
Microseismic and DAS help map fracture growth.
tip: R<sub>o</sub> ≈ 0.6–1.3% is the oil window; above about 1.3% is the gas window.

title: Digital oilfield
points: Sensors → SCADA/IIoT → historian → analytics and ML → decisions.
Data standards: WITSML (drilling), PRODML (production), RESQML (models).
Digital twins mirror assets using live data.
Fiber optics: DTS (temperature) and DAS (acoustic) along the whole well.
OT cybersecurity protects control systems.
tip: Garbage in, garbage out: data quality comes before any model.

title: Perforating
points: Shaped charge jet: entrance hole, tunnel, crushed zone.
Gun design choices: shot density (spf), phasing, charge type (deep penetrating or big hole).
Conveyance: wireline (fast, precise) or TCP (long intervals, high underbalance).
Underbalance cleans tunnels; overbalance needs other cleanup.
Correlate depth with GR and CCL before you shoot.
tip: Use big-hole charges for gravel packs and fracs, deep-penetrating charges for natural completions.

title: Oil and gas business
points: PRMS classes: reserves (1P, 2P, 3P), contingent resources, prospective resources.
Fiscal systems: concession (royalty plus tax), production sharing contract, service contract (Philippines).
Economic yardsticks: NPV, IRR, payout, profitability index.
Cost split: CAPEX (wells, facilities) versus OPEX (running costs, lifting cost).
6,000 scf ≈ 1 BOE.
tip: Draw the cash-flow diagram first, then discount each arrow.

title: Heavy oil
points: Heavy oil is below about 22 °API; extra-heavy is below 10 °API; bitumen does not flow at reservoir temperature.
Viscosity drops sharply with temperature, so thermal methods dominate.
SAGD (well pairs), CSS (huff and puff), steamflood, in-situ combustion.
Cold methods: CHOPS, PCP lift, diluent, VAPEX.
Efficiency is judged by the steam-oil ratio (lower is better).
equations: SOR = steam injected (CWE bbl) / oil produced (bbl)
tip: SOR of about 2–3 is good for SAGD; above about 4 is marginal.

title: General terms and units
points: 1 bbl = 42 US gal = 5.615 ft³ = 0.159 m³.
Standard conditions (US): 60 °F and 14.696 psia.
Mscf = thousand scf; MMscf = million scf.
Condensate drops out of gas; crude is liquid in the reservoir.
tip: Always write the units next to every number in an exam answer.
